newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran holds regional conference on Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Iran holds regional conference on Afghanistan.

text.p: Iran on Tuesday opened a regional conference to seek a solution to the Afghan crisis, but no Afghan factions are taking part and Pakistan, a key player, stayed away.

State-run Tehran radio said Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati opened the two-day conference, attended by delegates from the United Nations, Russia, China, India, Turkey, the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC) as well as Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan.
Journalists in Tehran said Velayati told a news conference that Ireland sent an official to represent the European Union.
Although invited to the conference, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Uzbekistan did not send delegates.
The ousted Afghan government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani, which Iran backs, was not taking part, the journalists said. Iran's media had earlier said it would send a delegation.

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Abbas Maleki told the Persian service of the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) that it was decided after consultation with other states to hold the conference without any of the Afghan factions present.
Iran's President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, speaking at an afternoon session, urged action by the U.N. and the OIC to resolve the Afghan crisis, Tehran radio reported.
"The crisis and insecurity in Afghanistan is detrimental not only to the region but also to world peace," he said.
Velayati earlier expressed hope that the session would lead to an international peace conference on Afghanistan.
He said any lasting solution to the war in Afghanistan "should come through the participation of all political and ethnic groups in an inter-Afghani dialogue".

Velayati said the United Nations had not done enough to draw world attention to the plight of Afghanistan's people and urged the world body to stop the intervention of "foreign countries in Afghanistan's internal affairs".

He was apparently referring to Pakistan, which the Iranian media have accused of setting up the Sunni Moslem Taleban with backing from the U.S. and funding from Saudi Arabia to counter Iran's influence in the region.
Pakistan, which plays an active role in Afghanistan, denies the charge and says it has no favourites among Afghan factions.
Pakistan said on Sunday it would not attend, citing problems with the agenda and guest list, which includes arch-foe India.

Velayati later told the news conference that Iran understood Pakistan's "important role" in Afghanistan and expressed hope that "in the future we will have Pakistan's contribution to regional cooperation".

Pakistan and Iran have been working closely together in diplomatic moves over Afghanistan during 17 years of civil war there, but differences appeared between them after the emergence of the Taleban as a new factor in Afghan politics.
Velayati reiterated that Iran, which last week branded Taleban as "rebels", recognised the Rabbani government.
He warned that if the fighting does not stop by the winter the world should expect to face "a more serious human tragedy in Afghanistan".
